analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers to arbitrate job disputes instead of going to court.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; after 58 Democrats signed on, it sat in committee for the remaining year and a half of the Congress and expired.
analysis.plain_summary: Most large employers require new hires to sign agreements sending any job dispute — discrimination, wage theft, harassment, firing — to a private arbitrator chosen under employer-friendly rules, instead of a public court, and often to give up the right to join with coworkers in a class action. This bill would void those agreements, allow arbitration only if a worker freely chooses it after a dispute has already arisen, with a 45-day waiting period and plain-language notice, ban retaliation against workers who refuse to arbitrate, and make it an unfair labor practice to force workers to give up group claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies with forced arbitration clauses — tens of millions of Americans — who would regain the right to have discrimination, harassment, and wage claims heard in court and to band together in class or collective actions. The bill expressly covers independent contractors regardless of what the employer labels them, and covers domestic workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with forced arbitration clauses, including contractors

how_it_helps.text: No predispute arbitration agreement requiring arbitration of a work dispute would be valid or enforceable; courts, not arbitrators, would decide whether an agreement qualifies [S3].

Post-dispute arbitration would be allowed only if voluntary: not a condition of employment, no coercion or threat of adverse action, plain-language written notice, at least a 45-day waiting period with the statute of limitations paused, and affirmative written consent [S3].
Employers could not retaliate against workers for refusing to arbitrate, and workers could sue for such retaliation with attorney's fees [S3].

The bill amends the National Labor Relations Act to make it an unfair labor practice to require or coerce employees to promise not to pursue joint, class, or collective claims, restoring the ability to band together [S3].
Independent contractors are covered no matter how the company classifies them, as are domestic workers in private households [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would lose a system that keeps most disputes out of court, caps damages, and bars group claims; companies would face more lawsuits, class actions, and public court records of workplace claims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers facing more court cases

drawbacks.text: Defenders of arbitration argue it is faster and cheaper for individual workers than court, which can take years and require lawyers; moving claims to court raises litigation costs for both sides and can mean workers with small claims recover less [S3] (the bill's own structure acknowledges court access as the remedy).

The 45-day waiting period and written-consent requirements would delay even genuinely voluntary post-dispute settlements, and the NLRA amendment reaches informal practices, giving employers new exposure to unfair-labor-practice charges [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: court is slower and costlier per case, but it is public, precedential, and open to group claims, while forced arbitration is private, individual, and decided under rules the employer sets. For disputes like discrimination and wage theft — where group claims and public accountability matter most — the balance favors the bill. The post-dispute carve-out with a 45-day cooling-off period is a careful design that keeps voluntary arbitration available.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Education and Labor Committees on the day it was introduced and, after being sent to a Judiciary subcommittee in June 2019, never got a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on May 15, 2019, with 49 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the Judiciary Committee and the Education and Labor Committee the same day [S5].
On June 26, 2019, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law — the last recorded action [S5].
58 Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
Neither committee ever reported the bill, and no vote was ever held on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers keep the existing system in which most large companies require workers to sign away their right to sue in court and to join class actions.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's sponsor and 58 cosponsors was a Democrat, and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.note: The bill voids the arbitration clauses these companies put in employment contracts, which currently keep disputes private, individual, and out of court. They would face more litigation, class actions, and public records of workplace claims.
A large share of the employment arbitration business comes from predispute clauses; banning those and requiring a 45-day voluntary post-dispute process would shrink the market.
Collective bargaining arbitration is expressly preserved, and the bill makes it an unfair labor practice for employers to block joint claims, strengthening workers' collective rights.
Restored court access and attorney's-fee provisions expand the market for worker-side representation.
